quote: Any politician who’d said “6,000 deaths is 1/8 the annual US casualties from automobile accidents,” would have been asked to resign the same hour.
content: One politician did dare. Barbara Lee cast the only vote in either house against the Authorization for Use of Military Force on September 14, 2001, said on the floor that the country should "not become the evil we deplore," received death threats, and was re-elected in 2002 with 81 percent of the vote and in every election since. The rally-round-the-flag surge is real and well documented (Mueller 1970), and the essay is right that it made restraint costly; but "no one would dare" and "asked to resign the same hour" are the essay's dramatization, and the one test case shows the cost was survivable. The essay's model of a spiral in which restraint is unspeakable predicts that Lee's career should have ended. Her district judged otherwise, which suggests that the audience for restraint existed and that the politicians who did not supply it were making a choice rather than obeying a law.

quote: If the USA had completely ignored the 9/11 attack—just shrugged and rebuilt the building—it would have been better than the real course of history.
content: This is a counterfactual stated with the confidence the essay is criticizing in others. The essay's argument requires only that the actual response was disproportionate, which the accounting supports; the wars that followed cost several trillion dollars and some seven thousand American service members, so the essay's "billions of dollars and thousands of soldiers' lives" understates the case by three orders of magnitude on the first figure, in an essay that opens by boasting that "ten times worse" was an understatement. Whether the null response would have been better depends on what al-Qaeda would have done next, which no one knows. The essay's sound point is that the vast majority of negative claims about any enemy are false and that "cowards" was one of them. Its unsound addition is a policy counterfactual delivered as fact, which is how the essay describes the other side's reasoning.
